lesson.title: Azure subscriptions management groups and landing zones
lesson.why: Growing from one subscription to many requires repeatable policy, ownership, networking, and billing boundaries. A landing zone is an operating foundation, not merely a diagram or deployment template.
lesson.what: Organize fictional Azure workloads using management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, platform services, and application landing zones.

concepts.name: Hierarchy determines inherited scope
concepts.body: Management groups organize subscriptions above the resource-group level. Azure RBAC and Policy assignments can inherit through their applicable scopes. A broad assignment high in the hierarchy affects many descendants, so placement deserves the same review as the policy definition itself.

concepts.name: Subscriptions are operational boundaries
concepts.body: Subscriptions provide resource organization, quota and billing relationships, and access scopes. They are not identical to Microsoft Entra tenants or invoices. Choose separation using workload lifecycle, compliance, scale, and team ownership rather than assuming every team needs an entirely separate tenant.

concepts.name: Platform and workload responsibilities differ
concepts.body: Platform landing zones provide shared connectivity, identity integration, management, and governance. Application landing zones host workloads within that foundation. A central platform should publish usable standards and escalation paths, while application owners remain responsible for service behavior and data handling.

concepts.name: Governance needs controlled exceptions
concepts.body: Preventive policies, auditing, budgets, and diagnostic settings support consistency, but not every control blocks deployment. Exemptions need owners and expiry. Moving a subscription between management groups can change inherited behavior, so migration requires a policy and access impact review.

e2e: List fictional workloads, data classifications, owners, and isolation requirements.
Choose subscription boundaries and management-group placement based on shared policy needs.
Assign platform versus application responsibilities for network, identity, monitoring, and recovery.
Canary inherited policy and access changes before broad rollout.
Review cost allocation and exceptions regularly, keeping an approved migration and rollback record.

tasks.name: Build a scoped hierarchy
steps: Sketch a tenant with Platform, Production, and Sandbox management groups and fictional subscriptions beneath them.
Place resource groups under subscriptions, not directly under management groups; identify the owner at each level.

tasks.name: Calculate shared allocation
steps: Assume a shared platform costs 1,200 fictional accounting units monthly and three workloads consume 50%, 30%, and 20% of its measured usage.
Expected allocations are 600, 360, and 240 units. These are invented accounting inputs, not Azure prices.

tasks.name: Evaluate inherited policy
steps: A sandbox subscription permits a resource region that the Production management group denies.
Explain that moving it requires impact review and potentially remediation; a resource group's local preference does not cancel an applicable inherited restriction.

tasks.name: Write an exception record
steps: Draft a hypothetical region-policy exemption with business reason, narrow scope, owner, expiry, and compensating controls.
These paper decisions do not establish actual RBAC or Policy behavior; future changes require approved tests.

key_terms: Management group: hierarchy scope organizing subscriptions.
Subscription: resource, access, quota, and billing-related boundary.
Resource group: lifecycle grouping of Azure resources.
Landing zone: governed foundation for hosting workloads.
Exemption: scoped exception to a policy assignment.
lesson.safety: Do not create subscriptions or move resources. Landing-zone deployments can create billable network, logging, and security services; broad inherited changes can disrupt many teams.
cleanup: Keep the fictional hierarchy and allocation assumptions.
No live hierarchy or policy assignments were changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a subscription move breaks deployments. How would you investigate without removing all governance?
interview_points: Compare inherited assignments before and after the move.
Inspect affected scopes and precise denial evidence.
Use a narrow reviewed exemption or corrected placement.
Clarify platform and workload ownership.

azure/azure-subscriptions-management-gro.core: Azure landing zones combine hierarchy and operating responsibilities. Management-group placement changes inheritance; subscriptions separate workloads and accountability. Canary governance changes and keep exceptions narrow and time-bound.

storyboard.title: A subscription inherits a new region policy
storyboard.objective: Connect hierarchy placement to deployment behavior.

scenes.title: Known placement
scenes.caption: The subscription follows its current inherited standards.
scenes.narration: Application owners deploy within the documented policy scope and use the platform team's published connectivity and monitoring foundation.

scenes.title: Move changes constraints
scenes.caption: A new ancestor can change allowed operations.
scenes.narration: After placement changes, a region restriction rejects the planned deployment even though its template has not changed.

scenes.title: Review scope and exception
scenes.caption: Governance recovery remains narrow and accountable.
scenes.narration: Owners compare inherited assignments, correct placement or approve a time-bound exemption, and verify both intended allows and denials.

lesson.title: Azure VMs VM Scale Sets and availability
lesson.why: A scale set can add machines without making an application resilient to a zone outage. Compute placement, health, startup, and state determine useful surviving capacity.
lesson.what: Compare individual VMs, scale-set orchestration, availability zones, and fault domains using a synthetic web workload and an offline capacity plan.

concepts.name: Scale sets manage a fleet
concepts.body: Virtual Machine Scale Sets organize VM instances and support scaling and lifecycle operations. Flexible and Uniform orchestration have different management models and supported combinations. Select the mode from workload and operational needs rather than assuming every example applies unchanged.

concepts.name: Failure domains are not interchangeable
concepts.body: Availability zones separate physical infrastructure within a supported region. Fault domains reduce certain correlated host failures but do not mean separate regions. Availability sets and zonal placement solve different scopes of risk; dependent disks and services must match the intended topology.

concepts.name: Scaling follows useful signals
concepts.body: Autoscale rules react to metrics or schedules within configured bounds. Startup scripts, image downloads, and application warmup delay useful capacity. A CPU threshold may miss queue backlog or memory bottlenecks, and quota availability can prevent a requested scale-out.

concepts.name: Health and state govern replacement
concepts.body: Application health signals and load-balancer probes influence routing and supported repair workflows. A healthy VM process can still be unable to serve requests. Externalize durable state and drain work before planned removal; local temporary storage should not hold irreplaceable records.

e2e: Record peak throughput, warmup time, state requirements, and failure tolerance.
Choose VM family, orchestration mode, and supported placement across failure domains.
Calculate surviving capacity before relying on reactive scaling.
Define probes, repair behavior, and autoscale bounds with dependency limits.
Rehearse replacement and rollback using an immutable image and application-level acceptance gates.

tasks.name: Map failure scope
steps: Draw six VMs distributed two per zone across three zones and identify a zonal database dependency.
Explain why compute diversity alone does not remove a database single point of failure.

tasks.name: Calculate zone-loss throughput
steps: Assume each VM safely serves 50 requests/second and demand is 180. Six VMs provide 300; losing one two-VM zone leaves 200.
Expected post-failure headroom is 20 requests/second. These hypothetical capacities require later representative measurement, not vendor guarantees.

tasks.name: Challenge a scaling metric
steps: A queue grows while CPU stays at 30% because workers wait on a slow dependency.
Investigate dependency latency and backlog rather than assuming a higher CPU threshold would detect the problem.

tasks.name: Plan an image rollout
steps: Canary a new image, verify readiness, and replace only a bounded number of VMs while preserving the zone-loss objective.
Retain the previous image reference. This offline plan does not test actual Azure capacity, repair, or authorization behavior.

key_terms: Scale set: managed group of VM instances.
Orchestration mode: scale-set lifecycle and management model.
Availability zone: regional infrastructure failure domain.
Warmup: time before new compute serves useful work.
Headroom: capacity exceeding required load.
lesson.safety: Do not create VMs or scale sets. Compute, disks, addresses, load balancers, and logs may incur costs even when application traffic is absent; deallocation does not remove every charge.
cleanup: Keep the capacity table and image rollback plan.
Future tests must inspect retained disks and network resources after deleting compute.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a VM scale set spans three zones but users still lose service during one-zone failure. What assumptions need checking?
interview_points: Calculate remaining measured throughput.
Find shared or zonal state dependencies.
Inspect health routing and startup delays.
Check quotas and orchestration-specific behavior.

azure/azure-vms-vm-scale-sets-and-availa.core: VM scale sets coordinate lifecycle and scaling, while placement and dependency design determine availability. Calculate surviving capacity, choose meaningful health signals, and keep state outside disposable compute.

storyboard.title: Azure VM scale-set capacity survives a zone loss
storyboard.objective: Connect placement, health, and spare throughput.

scenes.title: Balanced service
scenes.caption: Ready instances share demand across zones.
scenes.narration: The load balancer sends requests to healthy VMs while the fleet retains capacity above its measured normal demand.

scenes.title: A zone becomes unavailable
scenes.caption: Remaining capacity carries the immediate load.
scenes.narration: A zonal failure removes instances before replacements can warm up, so availability depends on surviving throughput and shared dependencies.

scenes.title: Restore measured headroom
scenes.caption: Scaling completes only when new VMs are useful.
scenes.narration: Replacement instances initialize and pass application checks, allowing the service to regain headroom without prematurely draining healthy capacity.

lesson.title: Azure Virtual Network routing private endpoints and DNS
lesson.why: A private endpoint can exist while clients still resolve the public service address. Private connectivity requires correct naming, routing, security controls, and service authorization together.
lesson.what: Trace a fictional application through a VNet to a private storage endpoint, including hybrid DNS and user-defined routes without touching live networking.

concepts.name: Effective routes determine the path
concepts.body: Azure combines system routes, user-defined routes, and learned routes according to documented selection rules. Longest-prefix matching is fundamental, with route-source precedence for ties. VNet peering provides connectivity but is not automatically transitive through another peered network.

concepts.name: Private endpoints map a service privately
concepts.body: A private endpoint provides a private IP interface for a supported service subresource through Private Link. It does not automatically disable the service's public endpoint or grant data permissions. Different subresources, such as blob and file, can require distinct endpoint and DNS configuration.

concepts.name: DNS must follow client location
concepts.body: Private DNS zones and VNet links can resolve service names to private addresses for linked networks. On-premises clients need suitable forwarding or resolver integration. Hard-coded private IPs bypass normal naming and TLS expectations and become fragile when endpoint configuration changes.

concepts.name: Security and routing are separate
concepts.body: NSGs, firewalls, endpoint-related network-policy settings, service access rules, and RBAC can each influence the request. A correct route does not imply authorization. Inspect supported private-endpoint policy behavior for the current configuration instead of applying generic subnet assumptions.

e2e: Resolve the service hostname from the client's actual DNS context.
Check private DNS records, zone links, and hybrid forwarding where applicable.
Inspect effective routes and confirm the destination matches the intended private endpoint.
Evaluate applicable network controls and service-side data authorization separately.
Validate both permitted access and blocked public paths in a later approved isolated test.

tasks.name: Draw a private storage path
tasks.goal: Separate name resolution from packet flow.
steps: Sketch application VNet, linked private DNS zone, storage private endpoint, and storage authorization.
Mark that endpoint creation alone does not disable public access or authorize the application.

tasks.name: Select a route offline
steps: Assume routes 10.0.0.0/8 to a hub, 10.20.0.0/16 to a specific peering, and 0.0.0.0/0 to a firewall.
For 10.20.3.4 the /16 wins; for 10.30.3.4 the /8 wins. This illustrative table omits real Azure route-source and special-route rules.

tasks.name: Diagnose hybrid DNS
steps: A VM resolves a storage name privately while an on-premises client resolves it publicly.
Inspect resolver forwarding and private-zone visibility before changing NSGs. Record expected private resolution for the intended client path.

tasks.name: Review isolation evidence
steps: List checks for public-network settings, endpoint subresource, DNS resolution, and a narrow data-role assignment.
State that this offline topology is not proof of live DNS, routing, or RBAC enforcement.

key_terms: VNet: Azure virtual network boundary.
UDR: user-defined route.
Private endpoint: private interface for a supported service.
Private DNS zone link: association enabling zone visibility to a VNet.
Peering: connection between virtual networks.
lesson.safety: Do not create endpoints or edit routes. Private Link, resolvers, firewalls, gateways, and transfer can incur costs; avoid opening public data access while troubleshooting.
cleanup: Retain the annotated DNS and packet paths.
No route, DNS, or endpoint changes require reversal.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a private endpoint works from Azure but not from an office network. Which evidence would you collect first?
interview_points: Compare DNS answers from both client contexts.
Inspect forwarding and private-zone links.
Trace effective routes and applicable network controls.
Check service authorization without treating connectivity as permission.

azure/azure-virtual-network-routing-priv.core: Azure private access needs DNS, route, endpoint subresource, network controls, and data authorization to agree. Creating Private Link does not automatically disable public access or solve hybrid resolution.

storyboard.title: Hybrid DNS misses an Azure private endpoint
storyboard.objective: Explain why client resolver context changes the destination.

scenes.title: Intended private lookup
scenes.caption: The hostname should resolve through private DNS.
scenes.narration: The office application asks its configured resolver for the storage hostname before attempting any connection to Azure.

scenes.title: Forwarding is absent
scenes.caption: Public resolution bypasses the intended private path.
scenes.narration: Without the necessary forwarding and zone visibility, the office client receives a public answer despite an existing private endpoint.

scenes.title: Repair resolver integration
scenes.caption: Use names consistently and retain authorization checks.
scenes.narration: Approved DNS integration supplies the private address, after which routing, network controls, and storage permissions still determine access.

lesson.title: Microsoft Entra ID Azure RBAC and managed identities
lesson.why: Obtaining a token does not mean an application may read every resource. Identity issuance, Azure resource authorization, and application data permissions must be evaluated separately.
lesson.what: Trace a managed identity requesting an Entra token and accessing Blob Storage using a narrowly scoped role assignment. All identities and resources are fictional.

concepts.name: Entra establishes identity
concepts.body: Microsoft Entra ID provides identity and token services. Tokens have an issuer, audience, expiry, and claims. A token for the wrong audience should not be accepted by a target service, even when it represents an otherwise valid identity.

concepts.name: RBAC binds principal, role, and scope
concepts.body: An Azure role assignment combines a security principal, role definition, and resource scope, with inheritance where applicable. Management-plane Actions and data-plane DataActions differ. Contributor-style resource management should not be mistaken for a direct grant to read every stored object.

concepts.name: Managed identities remove static credentials
concepts.body: System-assigned identities follow the lifecycle of their host resource. User-assigned identities are independent resources that can be attached to supported hosts. Both still need appropriate target authorization; assigning an identity is not equivalent to granting its access.

concepts.name: Least privilege includes lifecycle
concepts.body: Scope roles to required resources and actions, avoid unnecessary role-assignment administration, and review stale assignments. Permission changes and token caching can introduce propagation delays. Troubleshooting should inspect the actual principal and requested audience before rotating secrets that the design should not require.

e2e: Identify the workload and choose a system-assigned or user-assigned identity lifecycle.
Determine the exact target resource and required data operations.
Assign a suitable least-privilege role at the narrowest practical scope.
Have the workload obtain a target-audience token through its supported identity mechanism.
Validate intended reads and forbidden writes, accounting for propagation and cached credentials.

tasks.name: Choose identity lifecycle
steps: Compare one disposable VM with several independently replaced workers sharing an approved access profile.
Consider system-assigned identity for the first and carefully scoped user-assigned identity for the second; shared identity reduces per-worker attribution.

tasks.name: Work a role-scope table
tasks.goal: Predict a bounded offline authorization case.
steps: Assume a principal has only Storage Blob Data Reader on container reports and no other grants.

Expected design outcomes: read reports is permitted, write reports is not, and read another container is not. Actual service access also depends on network, conditions, and applicable authorization behavior.

tasks.name: Diagnose an audience mismatch
steps: A workload requests a token intended for Resource Manager and sends it to the storage data endpoint.
Identify the wrong audience rather than adding Owner. Record claim names only, never an actual bearer token.

tasks.name: Review removal and recovery
steps: Plan an access review covering deleted workloads, reusable identities, role scopes, and approved emergency access.
These mock decisions do not prove live RBAC, token propagation, or identity endpoint behavior.

key_terms: Principal: identity receiving authorization.
Audience: service a token is intended for.
Role assignment: binding of principal, role, and scope.
DataAction: role permission for supported data-plane operations.
Managed identity: Azure-managed workload identity without developer-held credentials.
lesson.safety: Do not obtain tokens or assign roles. Identity changes can expose data; subsequent authorized operations can incur service costs. Never paste tokens or real principal details into notes.
cleanup: Retain only fictional role-scope tables.
No credentials were created, retrieved, or stored.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a managed identity can deploy a storage account but cannot read blobs. Is the identity broken?
interview_points: Separate management-plane and data-plane permissions.
Verify principal, scope, and token audience.
Check networking and propagation.
Grant only justified data access rather than broad administration.

azure/microsoft-entra-id-azure-rbac-and-.core: Entra authenticates identities; Azure RBAC authorizes scoped operations. Managed identities eliminate stored workload secrets but still require correct role assignments and target-audience tokens. Management access is not automatically data access.

storyboard.title: A managed identity needs a data-plane role
storyboard.objective: Connect token issuance to scoped storage authorization.

scenes.title: Identity is established
scenes.caption: The workload receives a token for its target.
scenes.narration: The supported managed-identity mechanism supplies a token without requiring a password embedded in the application's configuration.

scenes.title: Data permission is missing
scenes.caption: A valid identity does not imply blob access.
scenes.narration: The storage request fails because the principal lacks the required data-plane role at the container's applicable scope.

scenes.title: Grant justified scope
scenes.caption: Read access remains distinct from write and administration.
scenes.narration: A reviewed container-scoped data-reader assignment enables intended reads while negative tests preserve the boundary against writes and other containers.

lesson.title: Azure Blob Storage Files and data protection
lesson.why: Storage redundancy does not protect against every accidental deletion, and a shared file protocol is not interchangeable with object APIs. Interface and recovery requirements should drive selection.
lesson.what: Compare Azure Blob Storage and Azure Files, then model redundancy, versioning, soft deletion, lifecycle, and restore evidence for synthetic documents.

concepts.name: Interface determines compatibility
concepts.body: Blob Storage exposes object-oriented APIs suited to whole-object access and metadata. Azure Files provides managed file shares through supported SMB or NFS configurations. A legacy application expecting file locking and directories may need Files rather than a superficial translation to blob names.

concepts.name: Redundancy addresses infrastructure failure
concepts.body: Locally, zone, and geographically redundant options protect against different failure scopes, subject to account and service support. Geo-replication can be asynchronous. Replicating a deletion or bad overwrite is not the same as maintaining independent historical recovery points.

concepts.name: Recovery features have scope
concepts.body: Blob versioning, blob and container soft delete, and point-in-time restore have distinct prerequisites and supported account configurations. Azure Files snapshots and backup offer different recovery workflows. Confirm feature compatibility instead of assuming one switch protects every storage interface and operation.

concepts.name: Retention changes the bill
concepts.body: Lifecycle rules can transition or delete eligible blob data, but retained versions and soft-deleted data can continue using billable storage. Archive access may require rehydration and has latency and cost implications. Immutable retention can prevent deletion, including during cleanup.

e2e: Choose object or file access from actual application protocol and locking requirements.
Select redundancy based on tolerated infrastructure failures and regional recovery needs.
Define version, deletion, and backup retention for supported features.
Calculate retained data and retrieval requirements before adding lifecycle transitions.
Rehearse restoration of a specific synthetic item and validate content, identity, and access permissions.

tasks.name: Choose the storage interface
steps: Compare an image API fetching entire objects with a legacy tool requiring SMB shared-folder access.
Select Blob as a candidate for the first and Azure Files for the second, then verify supported authentication and locking expectations.

tasks.name: Estimate retained data
steps: Assume 100 GB of current blob data and 8 GB of unique changed data retained daily for seven days.
An illustrative upper-level estimate is 100 + 8 x 7 = 156 GB, excluding redundancy accounting, metadata, and service-specific billing behavior; it is not a price quote.

tasks.name: Classify a deletion incident
steps: A user deletes a valid object and that state propagates to another region.
Choose an enabled historical recovery feature rather than claiming geo-redundancy preserves the old version automatically.

tasks.name: Review a lifecycle proposal
steps: An audit requires a file within minutes, but the proposed blob archive tier needs rehydration.
Reject the mismatch or revise the objective and retrieval design. Offline analysis does not prove actual restore timing or cloud permissions.

key_terms: Blob: object accessed through storage APIs.
File share: shared filesystem service.
Soft delete: recoverable retention after deletion.
Versioning: preservation of earlier object revisions.
Rehydration: making archived blob content available for online access.
lesson.safety: Do not create accounts or shares. Capacity, retained data, transactions, retrieval, backup, and transfer may incur costs; avoid immutable policies on disposable test data without review.
cleanup: Keep the recovery matrix for fictional documents.
Future test cleanup must inspect versions, snapshots, soft-deleted data, and retention locks rather than only current files.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a geo-redundant storage account loses a document after an accidental deletion. Why might redundancy not recover it?
interview_points: Deletion can replicate as a valid change.
Inspect enabled versioning, soft delete, snapshots, or backup.
Check feature scope and retention expiry.
Validate restored content and cost implications.

azure/azure-blob-storage-files-and-data-.core: Blob and Files solve different access semantics. Redundancy handles infrastructure failures; historical recovery needs compatible retention features. Include old versions, soft-deleted data, and archive retrieval in cost and recovery plans.

storyboard.title: A replicated deletion needs historical recovery
storyboard.objective: Show why redundancy is not an undelete feature.

scenes.title: Current document served
scenes.caption: The application uses the active object version.
scenes.narration: Normal document operations access current blob data while separately configured recovery features preserve eligible historical state.

scenes.title: Accidental deletion propagates
scenes.caption: A valid deletion is not a storage-hardware failure.
scenes.narration: The application deletes the document, and infrastructure redundancy can reproduce that change rather than retain an untouched current copy.

scenes.title: Restore retained content
scenes.caption: Recovery depends on prior configuration and retention.
scenes.narration: Operators select a recoverable historical version, restore it through the supported workflow, and verify bytes and application access.

lesson.title: Azure SQL Cosmos DB and managed databases
lesson.why: A managed database removes some infrastructure work, not the need to design transactions, access patterns, capacity, and recovery. Different consistency models change application behavior.
lesson.what: Compare relational Azure SQL choices with Cosmos DB's partitioned document model using an offline order workload and explicitly hypothetical capacity figures.

concepts.name: Relational compatibility matters
concepts.body: Azure SQL Database provides a managed relational engine, while SQL Managed Instance offers a different compatibility and operational surface. SQL Server on VMs leaves more administration to the customer. Choose using required features, transactions, migration constraints, and scaling rather than the word SQL alone.

concepts.name: Cosmos partition keys shape scale
concepts.body: A logical partition groups items by partition-key value, affecting transactional scope and request distribution. Hot partition keys can throttle while other capacity sits idle. Queries that fan out across partitions often consume more resources than point reads with both ID and partition key.

concepts.name: Consistency is an application contract
concepts.body: Cosmos DB offers strong, bounded staleness, session, consistent prefix, and eventual consistency with documented trade-offs. Session behavior depends on session context and tokens; it is not global strong consistency. Region topology and account configuration constrain available choices and latency.

concepts.name: Managed does not mean recovered
concepts.body: Backups, failover options, retention, and restore workflows differ between services and tiers. Measure restore and application reconnection against objectives. For Cosmos DB, request units reflect operation resource consumption, so indexing, query shape, item size, and consistency affect capacity demand.

e2e: List transaction boundaries, joins, access patterns, freshness, and engine compatibility requirements.
Choose relational or partitioned-document design based on these constraints.
Estimate workload capacity with representative operations rather than record count alone.
Define backup, regional failure, and application reconnect procedures for the selected service.
Validate correctness and performance using approved synthetic tests before migration.

tasks.name: Choose by transaction boundary
steps: Compare a financial ledger needing relational constraints and multi-row transactions with a document catalog mostly accessed by item and tenant.
Identify Azure SQL as a natural ledger candidate and Cosmos as a candidate requiring deliberate partition design for the catalog.

tasks.name: Calculate illustrative RU demand
steps: Assume measured example operations cost five RU each and arrive at 200/second. Modeled demand is 1,000 RU/second.
If a redesigned query costs 20 RU, demand becomes 4,000. These invented operation costs are arithmetic inputs, not Cosmos guarantees or prices.

tasks.name: Trace session freshness
steps: Client A writes a document and retains session context; client B reads using unrelated context.
Explain why a session guarantee for A should not be described as a global strong-read guarantee for B.

tasks.name: Plan recovery acceptance
steps: Specify an isolated restore, key business queries, partition distribution review, and client reconnection tests.
Document retention and regional assumptions. These offline decisions do not validate actual database consistency, throughput, or authorization.

key_terms: Relational constraint: database rule enforcing valid relationships or values.
Partition key: value grouping and distributing Cosmos items.
RU: normalized resource cost of an operation.
Session consistency: guarantees within a tracked client session.
PITR: restoration to an available earlier point.
lesson.safety: Do not create databases. Provisioned or serverless usage, replicas, backups, indexes, and transfer can cost money; never use production personal data in a trial migration.
cleanup: Retain fictional operation assumptions.
No database instances, accounts, or throughput settings were changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a Cosmos workload uses little aggregate throughput but one tenant is throttled. What design factors matter?
interview_points: Inspect partition-key concentration.
Compare point reads and fan-out queries.
Measure operation RU cost and indexing effects.
Preserve transaction and consistency requirements while redistributing work.

azure/azure-sql-cosmos-db-and-managed-da.core: Choose Azure SQL or Cosmos DB from data and transaction requirements. Cosmos partition keys, consistency, and operation RU costs drive behavior. Managed infrastructure still requires explicit recovery and application correctness tests.

storyboard.title: A Cosmos tenant saturates one partition key
storyboard.objective: Connect access pattern and request cost to capacity.

scenes.title: Expected access pattern
scenes.caption: Operations fit the original distribution assumption.
scenes.narration: Tenant requests use documented keys and consume capacity according to item size, indexing, consistency, and query work.

scenes.title: Hot tenant emerges
scenes.caption: Aggregate spare capacity can hide local pressure.
scenes.narration: One tenant concentrates expensive operations on a partition key, causing throttling even though other keys receive little traffic.

scenes.title: Revise with correctness constraints
scenes.caption: Optimization preserves transactional and freshness needs.
scenes.narration: Engineers reduce unnecessary query work and review partition design, then test the revised model without assuming throughput increases solve every hotspot.

lesson.title: Azure AKS and container operations
lesson.why: Kubernetes workloads can fail even when the AKS control plane is healthy. Operators must coordinate node pools, networking, image access, workload identity, and safe disruption.
lesson.what: Plan an AKS application rollout and node update using synthetic pod requests, subnet capacity, and readiness evidence rather than deploying a cluster.

concepts.name: Management has multiple boundaries
concepts.body: AKS manages Kubernetes control-plane capabilities while workload configuration, application behavior, and chosen compute/network settings remain important customer responsibilities. Automatic and Standard experiences expose different operational controls. Check current supported upgrade and networking combinations rather than copying a legacy cluster recipe.

concepts.name: Scheduling is constrained placement
concepts.body: Pod requests, taints, affinity, topology, and available addresses influence whether a pod can run. Limits and actual usage address different concerns. A pending pod is not always evidence of insufficient CPU; volumes, network setup, or placement rules may be the bottleneck.

concepts.name: Container access needs separate identities
concepts.body: Pulling images from Azure Container Registry and accessing application dependencies are separate authorization paths. Microsoft Entra Workload ID can federate Kubernetes service-account identity to Azure access where configured. Kubernetes RBAC still controls Kubernetes API operations rather than automatically granting Azure data permissions.

concepts.name: Upgrades require temporary capacity
concepts.body: Node surge settings provide replacement capacity during updates, consuming quota and addresses. Disruption budgets constrain voluntary evictions but do not stop unexpected failures. Readiness probes, compatible add-ons, and application tests must gate a rollout; a version update alone is not proof of successful service migration.

e2e: Inventory cluster experience, versions, node pools, networking, and workload ownership.
Check supported upgrade path, deprecated APIs, image compatibility, and add-on requirements.
Calculate surge, scheduling, address, and disruption headroom before replacement.
Update a bounded pool or canary and observe readiness, errors, and pending workloads.
Continue only after acceptance gates; retain documented workload and infrastructure recovery options.

tasks.name: Map identity paths
steps: Draw AKS pulling an image from ACR, then the application reading a Key Vault secret.
Assign separate permission checks and explain why successful image pulling does not prove the application can retrieve the secret.

tasks.name: Calculate surge demand
steps: Assume a ten-node pool and an illustrative 20% surge setting. Modeled extra nodes are two, making twelve during overlap.
If each node needs eight assumed address allocations, overlap adds sixteen. Actual Azure CNI address accounting depends on network mode and must be checked separately.

tasks.name: Diagnose a blocked drain
steps: Three replicas have minAvailable two, but one is already unready. The modeled voluntary disruption allowance is zero.
Repair readiness or add suitable capacity before expecting another eviction to succeed; do not remove the budget blindly.

tasks.name: Create a rollout gate
steps: Require a ready canary, successful synthetic requests, acceptable latency, and compatible system add-ons before expanding.
Document a stop and recovery path. This paper exercise does not prove actual AKS scheduling, federation, or upgrade behavior.

key_terms: Node pool: group of worker nodes with shared configuration.
Surge: temporary additional nodes during replacement.
Workload ID: federated application identity integration.
Readiness: ability to serve useful traffic.
Disruption budget: limit on voluntary pod unavailability.
lesson.safety: Do not create clusters or drain nodes. Node surge, disks, load balancers, registry storage, and telemetry can incur costs; use no production manifests containing secrets.
cleanup: Keep the synthetic headroom calculation.
Future cleanup must inspect persistent volumes and network resources, not just the cluster object.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, an AKS upgrade has spare CPU but cannot create replacements. What else could constrain it?
interview_points: Check surge quota and subnet/address capacity.
Inspect PDBs and existing unready pods.
Review taints, affinity, volumes, and add-ons.
Separate ACR access from runtime workload identity.

azure/azure-aks-and-container-operations.core: AKS operations combine version compatibility, workload readiness, network capacity, identities, and disruption limits. Surge consumes real temporary capacity. Test service behavior, not merely control-plane completion.

storyboard.title: AKS surge capacity meets an address limit
storyboard.objective: Connect upgrade overlap to networking capacity.

scenes.title: Prepare replacements
scenes.caption: The update requires temporary compute and networking.
scenes.narration: The node-pool rollout requests surge capacity so new nodes can become ready before old capacity leaves service.

scenes.title: Address allocation fails
scenes.caption: CPU headroom does not guarantee network headroom.
scenes.narration: The configured subnet or pod-address plan lacks necessary spare addresses, preventing replacement workloads from starting as expected.

scenes.title: Restore prerequisites
scenes.caption: Resume only after networking and readiness checks.
scenes.narration: Operators correct the approved capacity plan and verify replacement readiness before allowing the rollout to remove existing nodes.

lesson.title: Azure Functions App Service and Container Apps
lesson.why: Different managed hosting options optimize different workloads. Event-driven code, conventional web applications, and container revisions have distinct scaling, networking, and lifecycle constraints.
lesson.what: Select among Functions, App Service, and Container Apps for a fictional API and worker system using runtime needs and operating requirements rather than a universal favorite.

concepts.name: Functions centers on triggers
concepts.body: Azure Functions executes code from supported triggers and bindings. Hosting plan and trigger type affect scaling, execution constraints, networking, and retry behavior. Functions are not automatically exactly once; event handlers need idempotency and durable external state.

concepts.name: App Service hosts applications
concepts.body: App Service supports managed web application hosting with plan-based compute and deployment capabilities. Supported deployment slots help stage changes, but configuration swaps and database schema compatibility need review. Running a web app does not automatically provide queue-worker semantics or unlimited background execution.

concepts.name: Container Apps operates revisions
concepts.body: Container Apps runs containerized applications and jobs with managed ingress and event-driven scaling options. Revisions support controlled traffic movement where applicable. Minimum replicas, workload profiles, ingress, and scaling rules determine cold-start behavior and cost; scale-to-zero is not universal across all configurations.

concepts.name: Dependencies set the real ceiling
concepts.body: A rapidly scaling front end can exhaust database connections or downstream quotas. Bound concurrency and make startup deterministic. Durable data belongs in appropriate external storage, and secrets should use supported identity-based access rather than being copied into container images or deployment packages.

e2e: Describe protocol, trigger, runtime, duration, state, and scaling requirements.
Choose a hosting option and plan whose documented limits fit the workload.
Define identity, network, observability, and downstream concurrency constraints.
Deploy a hypothetical immutable version and shift traffic only after readiness tests.
Plan application and schema rollback together, accounting for persistent data outside compute.

tasks.name: Match three workloads
steps: Assign a timer-triggered cleanup function, a conventional framework web app, and a containerized queue worker to candidate hosting options.
Explain Functions, App Service, and Container Apps as candidates, then list one plan or runtime constraint that could change each choice.

tasks.name: Calculate downstream pressure
steps: Assume each replica opens eight database connections and the application budget is 80 connections.
Ten replicas consume the budget; reserve 16 connections for maintenance to reduce the modeled limit to eight replicas. Real pooling and transient overlap require measurement.

tasks.name: Design a revision gate
steps: For a container API, propose sending a small synthetic traffic share to a new revision and comparing errors and latency.
Do not interpret successful container startup as proof that authentication, schema compatibility, and dependencies work.

tasks.name: Review an event retry
steps: A function writes a record and crashes before acknowledging its trigger. Keep a stable event identifier and a durable duplicate check.
This mock does not prove real trigger retries, hosting limits, or cloud permissions.

key_terms: Trigger: event source starting a function.
Hosting plan: resource and feature envelope for execution.
Revision: immutable Container Apps application version.
Slot: supported staged App Service deployment target.
Concurrency: work active simultaneously.
lesson.safety: No hosting resources are created. Minimum instances, plans, execution, logs, networking, and databases may cost money even at low traffic; do not assume scale-to-zero makes everything free.
cleanup: Retain the workload decision table.
Future tests must remove unused revisions, plans, jobs, and retained logs according to their actual lifecycle.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a managed application scales successfully but its database fails. What is the architecture missing?
interview_points: Budget database connections and request concurrency.
Account for replica overlap and cold starts.
Use queueing or load shedding where appropriate.
Choose hosting features from workload requirements, not branding.

azure/azure-functions-app-service-and-co.core: Functions emphasizes triggers, App Service managed web hosting, and Container Apps container revisions and event scaling. Plans and dependencies constrain all three. Bound concurrency, externalize state, and make retries idempotent.

storyboard.title: Container scaling exhausts database connections
storyboard.objective: Show why managed scaling still needs dependency limits.

scenes.title: Normal replicas
scenes.caption: Current connection demand fits the budget.
scenes.narration: Application replicas serve requests using bounded pools while the database retains enough capacity for normal operations.

scenes.title: Scale-out amplifies connections
scenes.caption: Compute growth can overload a shared dependency.
scenes.narration: More replicas initialize pools simultaneously, exceeding the database connection budget even though application compute remains available.

scenes.title: Bound and recover
scenes.caption: Replica limits and pooling protect useful throughput.
scenes.narration: The team constrains replica concurrency, reserves maintenance headroom, and uses queueing or load shedding while restoring healthy database access.

lesson.title: Azure Service Bus Event Hubs and Event Grid
lesson.why: Business commands, telemetry streams, and resource notifications have different retention and consumption needs. Using one messaging product for all three can obscure ordering and recovery responsibilities.
lesson.what: Compare Service Bus, Event Hubs, and Event Grid, then trace acknowledgement, checkpointing, retries, and duplicate handling with synthetic messages.

concepts.name: Service Bus handles enterprise messages
concepts.body: Queues distribute work; topics and subscriptions support independent consumers. Peek-lock processing separates receipt from completion, and locks can expire. Sessions provide ordered processing within a session scope where supported, but a lock or duplicate-detection feature does not atomically include external business writes.

concepts.name: Event Hubs stores partitioned streams
concepts.body: Producers append events to partitions, and consumer groups maintain independent views of progress. Checkpoints record application progress so processing can resume. Ordering is partition-scoped, and replay is possible within retention; it is not a queue that deletes each event after one consumer reads it.

concepts.name: Event Grid routes discrete events
concepts.body: Event Grid distributes notifications to subscribers using supported delivery models. Filters select relevant events; retry and dead-letter configuration determine failure handling. Subscribers should expect duplicates and validate event schemas rather than infer business completion from successful publication.

concepts.name: Acknowledge after durable work
concepts.body: Crashing after a database commit but before message completion or checkpointing can repeat processing. Stable business identifiers and durable idempotency protect effects. Poison messages need quarantine and controlled replay; continuously retrying malformed data consumes capacity without improving correctness.

e2e: Classify each payload as a command, stream record, or event notification.
Choose service and partition/session scope from ordering, replay, and consumer needs.
Define completion or checkpoint timing after durable idempotent processing.
Set retention, retry, and failure-destination policies with owner alerts.
Replay synthetic failures at a bounded rate after fixing the cause and preserving duplicate protection.

tasks.name: Match services to intent
steps: Assign invoice processing, device telemetry analytics, and blob-created notification to candidate services.
Expected candidates are Service Bus, Event Hubs, and Event Grid respectively; explain the requirement behind each rather than claiming exclusivity.

tasks.name: Calculate stream replay
steps: Assume 90,000 retained events remain, consumers process 600/second, and producers add 300/second.
Net catch-up is 300/second, giving 300 seconds or five minutes. If retention expires first, this model cannot recover missing history.

tasks.name: Trace checkpoint ambiguity
steps: An Event Hubs consumer stores event E's result but crashes before saving its checkpoint.
On restart E may be replayed. Require a durable event or business key rather than treating a checkpoint as an external transaction guarantee.

tasks.name: Design poison-message recovery
steps: A schema-invalid invoice repeatedly fails. Route it to an appropriate dead-letter or quarantine workflow and alert an owner.
Test a repaired synthetic payload before replay. These mocks do not prove real locks, delivery ordering, or Azure authorization.

key_terms: Peek-lock: receive mode reserving a message before completion.
Session: scoped ordered Service Bus processing group.
Partition: ordered append stream segment.
Consumer group: independent stream-consumption view.
Checkpoint: persisted processing position.
lesson.safety: Do not publish or replay real messages. Throughput capacity, requests, retention, capture, and downstream processing can incur costs or repeat real business actions.
cleanup: Discard synthetic event and invoice identifiers.
Future test cleanup must inspect retained messages, subscriptions, and capture storage independently.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a telemetry consumer repeats records after restart. Why might this be expected rather than a broker defect?
interview_points: Checkpointing may lag durable processing.
Ordering and replay are partition-scoped.
Idempotency belongs at the external business effect.
Check retention and recovery throughput before promising catch-up.

azure/azure-service-bus-event-hubs-and-e.core: Service Bus manages business messages, Event Hubs partitioned streams, and Event Grid notifications. Completion and checkpoints can lag side effects, so duplicate-safe processing and controlled replay remain essential.

storyboard.title: An Event Hubs consumer resumes before its last commit

scenes.title: Process a partition
scenes.caption: The consumer advances through retained records.
scenes.narration: Telemetry processing writes useful results and periodically records progress for its independent consumer-group view of the partition.

scenes.title: Crash before progress is saved
scenes.caption: The next start can revisit already processed records.
scenes.narration: A result is durable but its checkpoint is not, so recovery begins from an earlier recorded position.

scenes.title: Replay without duplicate effects
scenes.caption: Stable identifiers distinguish prior completion.
scenes.narration: The restarted consumer recognizes completed event effects, processes remaining work, and advances its checkpoint only after durable success.

lesson.title: Azure Monitor Log Analytics and Application Insights
lesson.why: Infrastructure metrics can look healthy while customers experience slow dependencies. A useful observability design connects request outcomes, distributed traces, structured logs, and actionable alerts.
lesson.what: Combine Azure Monitor, Log Analytics, and Application Insights using fabricated request records. Keep sampling, retention, query scope, and privacy explicit.

concepts.name: Azure Monitor is the broader platform
concepts.body: Azure Monitor brings metrics, logs, traces, and alerting together. Platform collection and application instrumentation have different configuration needs. Do not assume every desired guest log or resource diagnostic is already collected merely because the resource appears in the portal.

concepts.name: Log Analytics queries retained records
concepts.body: A workspace provides a query and retention context for supported log tables. KQL filters and summarizes records, but table choice, time range, ingestion delay, and schema affect results. An empty result can indicate collection gaps rather than a healthy application.

concepts.name: Application Insights connects requests
concepts.body: Application Insights captures application performance signals through supported instrumentation, including request and dependency relationships. Distributed trace context connects spans across services. Sampling reduces volume but can affect naive counts and rare-error visibility; understand the sampling representation before computing business totals.

concepts.name: Alerts need actionable meaning
concepts.body: Alert thresholds require meaningful aggregation, evaluation windows, and missing-data handling. A high CPU alert is not a complete customer-impact signal. Pair service-level error and latency signals with diagnostic telemetry, clear ownership, and a runbook that avoids exposing secrets.

e2e: Define customer-facing success and latency objectives and identify the request path.
Instrument supported request and dependency telemetry with safe correlation identifiers.
Configure needed diagnostics, collection rules, workspace retention, and sampling deliberately.
Query a bounded time range, correlate slow dependencies, and distinguish absence from missing collection.
Create actionable alerts and validate their expected behavior with synthetic observations.

tasks.name: Map a trace
steps: Sketch browser request, API span, database span, and external-call span with a shared trace context.
Explain why a slow request can occur at low host CPU when it waits on another service.

tasks.name: Calculate an error percentage
steps: Use 400 successful and 20 failed unsampled requests. Total is 420 and failure percentage is 20 / 420 x 100 = 4.7619%.
Do not divide failures only by successes, and do not apply this unweighted calculation blindly to sampled telemetry.

tasks.name: Review an empty query
steps: A five-minute query returns no records. Check workspace, table, time range, ingestion delay, and instrumentation status.
Write two possible explanations: no traffic or missing collection; the result alone cannot distinguish them.

tasks.name: Draft an alert contract
steps: Specify a hypothetical sustained error-ratio threshold, minimum traffic, evaluation window, owner, and first diagnostic query.
This paper design does not prove live alert delivery, instrumentation, or cloud access. Use synthetic identifiers and exclude personal payloads.

key_terms: Workspace: log storage and query context.
KQL: query language for filtering and analyzing telemetry.
Span: timed operation within a trace.
Sampling: retaining selected telemetry with known representation.
Ingestion delay: time before emitted telemetry becomes queryable.
lesson.safety: Do not query production telemetry or enable collection. Ingestion, retention, queries, exports, and alerts can cost money; redact authorization headers, secrets, and personal information.
cleanup: Discard fabricated request records.
Keep collection assumptions and alert ownership; no telemetry settings were changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, customers report timeouts but a Log Analytics query is empty. What should you conclude?
interview_points: Do not conclude the service is healthy.
Check collection, scope, time range, and ingestion delay.
Correlate request and dependency traces.
Account for sampling and protect sensitive telemetry.

azure/azure-monitor-log-analytics-and-ap.core: Azure Monitor combines operational signals; Log Analytics queries retained logs and Application Insights links application requests and dependencies. Collection scope, sampling, and delay constrain conclusions and alert calculations.

storyboard.title: Application Insights reveals a slow dependency
storyboard.objective: Connect request symptoms to trace evidence.

scenes.title: Normal request trace
scenes.caption: Request and dependency timings share context.
scenes.narration: The application emits correlated observations so operators can relate user-facing duration to the work performed by dependencies.

scenes.title: Dependency wait dominates
scenes.caption: Low CPU does not imply low user latency.
scenes.narration: An external call slows down and extends request duration while the API spends little CPU time doing active computation.

scenes.title: Query with collection context
scenes.caption: Evidence is interpreted with sampling and ingestion limits.
scenes.narration: Operators query the correct workspace and time range, compare dependency spans, and verify collection completeness before selecting mitigation.

lesson.title: Azure Key Vault and policy governance
lesson.why: A vault can have strong cryptography yet weak access governance or an incomplete recovery plan. Policy compliance, data authorization, network access, and deletion protection address different risks.
lesson.what: Design a fictional application's Key Vault access and recovery controls, then evaluate Azure Policy effects without retrieving or changing any real secret.

concepts.name: Vault objects have distinct purposes
concepts.body: Key Vault manages keys, secrets, and certificates. Key operations can protect cryptographic use without exporting key material, while secrets are retrieved values. Supported authorization models and roles determine who can administer the vault versus use its data.

concepts.name: Identity and network are separate gates
concepts.body: A managed identity can authenticate without a stored password but still needs a suitable data-plane role or applicable configured permission. Network restrictions and private endpoint DNS can independently deny access. Broad management permission is not a reason to bypass data authorization.

concepts.name: Deletion protection needs recovery planning
concepts.body: Soft delete retains deleted vaults and objects for a configured recovery interval. Purge protection prevents premature permanent deletion within its enforced retention. Recovering a vault does not automatically restore every integration, such as role assignments or Event Grid subscriptions; those dependencies require review.

concepts.name: Policy effects differ
concepts.body: Azure Policy can audit, deny, modify, or deploy related configuration through supported effects. An audit finding reports noncompliance rather than blocking every operation. Remediation may require a managed identity and permissions; exemptions and assignment scope determine where a rule actually applies.

e2e: Inventory fictional keys, secrets, certificates, consumers, and recovery dependencies.
Assign narrow data access and separate administrative duties at appropriate scopes.
Choose network restrictions and DNS integration compatible with legitimate consumers.
Apply reviewed deletion protection and policy assignments with explicit effect and exemption handling.
Rehearse object and vault recovery, including authorization and integration restoration checks.

tasks.name: Separate permissions
steps: List vault configuration management, reading one secret, and performing a key-signing operation.
Require separate justified permissions rather than one broad owner role for every consumer.

tasks.name: Work a retention decision
steps: Assume a hypothetical 30-day protected recovery interval and accidental deletion detected on day 12.
There are 18 days remaining in this simplified timeline. Escalate recovery now; do not assume retention renews merely because someone noticed the deletion.

tasks.name: Compare audit and deny
steps: A policy audits missing purge protection and reports a vault noncompliant. Explain why an audit effect is not equivalent to rejecting its creation.
Propose a narrowly tested stronger effect only if the supported policy and operational requirements justify it.

tasks.name: Rehearse vault recovery
tasks.goal: Recover dependencies as well as objects.
steps: List object recovery, data-role assignments, private DNS, subscriptions, and application authentication checks.
State that recovering the vault alone may not restore integrations. This mock does not validate real Key Vault or Policy enforcement.

key_terms: Secret: protected retrievable value.
Data-plane role: authorization for vault-object use.
Soft delete: recoverable deleted state.
Purge protection: prevention of early permanent deletion.
Policy effect: action taken when a policy condition matches.
lesson.safety: Never retrieve secrets or practice key deletion. Vault operations, certificates, networking, and diagnostics can cost money; deletion can compromise backup recovery or application availability.
cleanup: Keep fictional dependency names only.
No secret values, policies, role assignments, or vaults were changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a deleted vault is recovered but its application still gets denied. What might recovery have omitted?
interview_points: Review data-role assignments and integrations.
Check private DNS and network restrictions.
Verify actual identity and object version.
Separate policy compliance from runtime authorization.

azure/azure-key-vault-and-policy-governa.core: Key Vault needs data authorization, network access, and recoverable lifecycle controls. Azure Policy effects are not interchangeable. Vault recovery must include role assignments and integrations, not just recovered secret objects.

storyboard.title: Recovered Key Vault still needs access restoration
storyboard.objective: Show why object recovery is not complete application recovery.

scenes.title: Authorized secret use
scenes.caption: Identity and data-role scope permit the request.
scenes.narration: The application retrieves its required secret through an approved identity and network path without storing a long-lived access key.

scenes.title: Vault deletion interrupts service
scenes.caption: Recovery must consider attached integrations.
scenes.narration: Accidental deletion stops access, and restoring the vault does not necessarily recreate the role assignments and integrations previously attached to it.

scenes.title: Restore and verify dependencies
scenes.caption: Objects, permissions, and connectivity are checked together.
scenes.narration: Operators recover the protected vault, restore reviewed access assignments, and validate application retrieval without exposing the secret value.

lesson.title: Azure Bicep ARM and deployment operations
lesson.why: Declarative deployment reduces manual drift but does not make changes risk-free or transactional. A preview, a successful resource deployment, and a working application are different milestones.
lesson.what: Trace Bicep source through ARM deployment planning and resource-provider operations. Review synthetic changes offline without running Azure deployment commands.

concepts.name: Bicep expresses desired resources
concepts.body: Bicep is a declarative language compiled into ARM template form. Parameters, modules, symbolic references, and outputs structure reusable definitions. Explicit API versions and resource properties matter because providers evolve; syntactically valid source can still describe an unsupported or unsafe configuration.

concepts.name: Dependencies organize operations
concepts.body: References can establish resource dependencies, allowing independent operations to proceed concurrently. Existing-resource declarations reference infrastructure without creating it. Dependency ordering does not guarantee application readiness, DNS convergence, or successful authentication immediately after the provider reports completion.

concepts.name: What-if is a prediction
concepts.body: ARM what-if previews proposed resource changes without applying them, but it calls Azure and needs appropriate permissions. Some expressions and provider defaults can produce incomplete or noisy differences. A clean preview is not proof of deployment success, available quota, or application correctness.

concepts.name: Deletion and rollback need intent
concepts.body: Incremental deployment is not a patch that ignores omitted properties on resources being redeployed; provider defaults can reset settings. Omitted resources have different handling from omitted properties. Deletion workflows, deployment stacks, and legacy complete-mode behavior require explicit review, and failed deployments can leave partial changes.

e2e: Define the deployment scope, ownership, parameters, and existing dependencies.
Compile and lint source locally, avoiding secret values in files and outputs.
Review an authorized what-if when later approved, classifying replacements and destructive changes.
Deploy through a controlled pipeline with scoped permissions and recorded versions.
Validate resource and application behavior, then reconcile partial changes or execute the documented recovery plan.

tasks.name: Draw a dependency graph
steps: Sketch VNet, subnet, private endpoint, and application references in a fictional Bicep module graph.
Identify which references establish deployment dependencies and which later checks still require DNS or application readiness evidence.

tasks.name: Classify a synthetic preview
steps: Assume a preview shows Create diagnostic setting, Modify storage TLS minimum, and Delete production database.
Expected decision: block approval because the database deletion lacks explicit intent and recovery evidence. The harmless create does not cancel the destructive change.

tasks.name: Find an omitted-property risk
tasks.goal: Avoid treating incremental as a partial patch.
steps: A redeployed resource definition omits a previously configured property. Flag the need to inspect provider default and template behavior.
Distinguish this from a resource entirely absent from an incremental template; the two omissions are not equivalent.

tasks.name: Plan partial-failure recovery
steps: Suppose networking succeeds but application creation fails. Inventory the successful changes before retrying or reverting.
Use versioned inputs and protect persistent data. Offline review does not validate real ARM what-if, provider behavior, or permissions.

key_terms: Bicep: declarative Azure infrastructure language.
ARM: Azure Resource Manager deployment and management layer.
Resource provider: service implementing a resource type.
What-if: predicted deployment change set.
Incremental mode: deployment mode retaining unspecified resources while redeploying specified definitions.
lesson.safety: Do not run what-if or deployments in this lesson. Real deployments can create charges or delete resources; never emit secrets in deployment outputs or commit parameter credentials.
cleanup: Keep the synthetic change-review decision.
No Azure resources or deployment records were created; remove only local scratch diagrams.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, an incremental Bicep deployment resets a property and then fails halfway. Why is automatic full rollback an unsafe assumption?
interview_points: Specified resources can have omitted properties reset by provider behavior.
Deployment operations are not one application transaction.
Inventory partial success and protect persistent data.
Use previews, versioned inputs, and explicit recovery procedures.

azure/azure-bicep-arm-and-deployment-ope.core: Bicep declares desired infrastructure for ARM. What-if predicts changes but uses cloud permissions and is not proof of success. Incremental deployment does not make omitted properties harmless, and partial failure needs explicit recovery.

storyboard.title: ARM deployment succeeds only partially
storyboard.objective: Separate declarative intent from transactional assumptions.

scenes.title: Reviewed resource plan
scenes.caption: Dependencies organize provider operations.
scenes.narration: The deployment submits versioned desired state and creates network prerequisites before attempting the dependent application resource.

scenes.title: Application creation fails
scenes.caption: Earlier successful changes can remain present.
scenes.narration: The application provider rejects its operation after networking succeeds, leaving a partial deployment rather than an automatic global rollback.

scenes.title: Reconcile from evidence
scenes.caption: Retry or rollback follows an inventory of actual state.
scenes.narration: Operators inspect completed operations, correct the failed declaration, and choose a controlled retry or recovery without deleting persistent dependencies blindly.
